title: Passive quantum memory in three dimensions
formal: Does there exist a family of three-dimensional, bounded-density local Pauli stabilizer Hamiltonians \(H_{n}\) and a fixed inverse temperature \(0<\beta <\infty\) for which the lifetime \(\tau _{n}(\beta )\) of one encoded qubit, under the thermal dynamics below and without intervention during storage, tends to infinity as \(n\to \infty\)?
definitions: The family may use an unbounded subsequence of qubit counts n. Place the qubits in \(\mathbb{R} ^{3}\), with at most B qubits in each unit ball. Let \(H_{n}=\sum_{j}(I- S_{j})/2\), where the \(S_{j}\) are commuting nonidentity Hermitian Pauli checks, each supported in a ball of radius R, each qubit belongs to at most B checks, and their joint +1 eigenspace has dimension two. B and R are constants independent of n. A Pauli check is a signed tensor product of I,X,Y,Z; X flips |\(0\rangle\) and |\(1\rangle , Z\) changes the sign of |\(1\rangle\), and Y=iXZ. Use the following fixed Davies-type thermal generator, in units with ℏ=\(k_{B}=1\). If \(\Pi _{E}\) is the energy-E spectral projector of \(H_{n}\), define \(A_{i,\mathrm{P},\omega}=\sum_{E' - E=\omega}\Pi _{E'}\mathrm{P}_{i}\Pi _{E}\) for every qubit \(i, \mathrm{P}\in \{X,Y,Z\}\), and energy difference \(\omega\). Put \(g\beta (\omega )=\min \{1,\exp (- \beta \omega )\}\) and \(\mathrm{L}_{n},\beta (\rho )=- i[H_{n},\rho ]+\sum_{i,\mathrm{P},\omega}g\beta (\omega )[A\rho A\dagger - (A\dagger A\rho +\rho A\dagger A)/2]\), with \(A=A_{i,\mathrm{P},\omega}\) in each summand. Its evolution is \(\Phi _{n},\beta ,t=\exp (tL_{n},\beta )\). Every single-qubit Pauli error is coupled to the bath; energy-raising rates are positive, and attempt rates do not shrink with system size. Choose a completely positive trace-preserving encoding map Enc\(_{n},\beta\) from one-qubit states to n-qubit states, with a completely positive trace-preserving left inverse at \(t=0\). It may use a thermal auxiliary state and need not be efficiently preparable. For this fixed encoding, let \(\varepsilon _{n},\beta (t)=\inf _{D} \sup _{\rho} \Vert D\circ \Phi _{n},\beta ,t\circ\)Enc\(_{n},\beta (\rho )- \rho \Vert _{1}\), where \(\rho\) ranges over all one-qubit density matrices, D over recovery channels from n qubits to one, and \(\Vert A\Vert _{1}=Tr\sqrt{A\dagger A}\). Define \(\tau _{n}(\beta )=\inf \{t\ge 0:\varepsilon _{n},\beta (t)>1/10\}\), with infimum of the empty set equal to infinity. Encoding happens before storage and recovery only at the end. This card fixes a stabilizer and thermal-bath model for the broader physical existence question; it imposes neither translation invariance nor a symmetry restriction on allowed errors.
answer_criterion: Prove existence of a family, one fixed finite \(\beta\), and encodings with \(\tau _{n}(\beta )\to \infty\), or prove that no family in this stated model has that property. A bound \(\exp (\Omega (n^{\eta}))\) for a fixed \(\eta >0\) would be stronger than required. A lifetime improving only up to a temperature-dependent maximum system size does not suffice. Cooling the bath as n grows, increasing local interaction strengths, slowing error rates with n, enforcing an error-forbidding symmetry, or applying active correction during storage changes the target.
why: A foundational question about whether quantum information can enjoy passive thermal protection in physical three-dimensional space. The recent claimed solution makes careful separation of storage, initialization, bath restrictions and stability especially important.

importance.reason: A defining problem at the intersection of quantum information and many-body physics; retained with an explicit claimed-resolution flag to preserve its history and prevent misleading open-status selection.

progress.text: Chesi and coauthors formulate thermodynamic criteria and relaxation bounds for stabilizer and subsystem quantum memories.
Brown and coauthors survey passive thermal memories, dimensional restrictions and proposed ways around them.
Stahl–Nandkishore prove symmetry-protected three-dimensional memory mechanisms with constrained dynamics.
The cored-product revision reports finite-size evidence on memories up to 60,000 qubits.
Balasubramanian–Davydova–Lin claim an affirmative solution with thermal encoding and stretched-exponential lifetime.
Williamson’s layer-code result appears in PRL; its guarantee is partial self-correction over a temperature-dependent size regime.

status_note: Claimed affirmative resolution in arXiv:2605.10943, 11 May 2026, for passive storage with thermal encoding. Its assumptions and stated theorems were checked, but the full proof was not independently verified. This is not labelled confirmed open. Review cutoff: 11 September 2026.

context_blocks.text: This record now has a claimed affirmative resolution. Balasubramanian, Davydova and Lin’s May 2026 preprint presents local three-dimensional stabilizer Hamiltonians with lifetime \(\exp (\Omega (n^{\eta}))\) at sufficiently low fixed temperature, for some \(\eta >0\). Its initialization is a thermal encoding. The catalogue flags this as a recent proof claim whose complete argument has not been independently verified here, rather than continuing to present the broad existence problem as confidently open.

A passive memory asks the Hamiltonian and its thermal environment to preserve information between an initial encoding and a final recovery. No repeated syndrome measurements or corrections are performed during storage. Quantum information requires preserving arbitrary superpositions, not only two distinguishable classical states. A material can preserve whether it is mostly magnetized up or down while rapidly losing the phase between those two possibilities; such a material is a classical memory, not a qubit memory.

The bath must be part of the mathematical specification. If errors that change the logical information are simply forbidden, a long lifetime may reflect that restriction. If every local transition is slowed as the device grows, a divergent lifetime can be manufactured by changing the clock. The generator above fixes the time scale and includes all single-qubit Pauli couplings, with ordinary positive-temperature suppression of energy-raising transitions.

An energy barrier is informative but does not alone determine memory time. A logical error may require crossing a high-energy configuration, yet the number of routes and intermediate configurations can be so large that entropy offsets the energetic suppression. Thermodynamic stability criteria therefore use both the bath dynamics and the thermal probability of configurations on which a recovery rule becomes unstable. A recovery map used to analyze the information is compatible with passive storage when it is applied only at readout.

The order of limits matters. Williamson’s layer-code result, published in August 2026, proves a regime in which lifetime grows exponentially with linear system size, but only up to a length scale exponential in inverse temperature. The lifetime at that crossover is very large as temperature falls. For the present question, however, temperature is fixed while system size goes to infinity, so an improvement restricted to a finite crossover regime is partial self-correction.

Roberts, Koh, Tan and Yao’s cored product codes take a different route using disordered geometry. Their January 2026 revision reports finite-temperature simulations of a pinwheel-based three-dimensional memory with up to 60,000 qubits, finding evidence that lifetime increases with size below a critical temperature. Those numerical results motivate a candidate construction but cannot by themselves establish the infinite-family limit required here.

Stahl and Nandkishore obtain protection in three dimensions by enforcing a one-form symmetry on the dynamics, even when enforcement is confined to a subvolume of vanishing relative size. This is a meaningful mechanism, but it restricts which local errors the environment may produce. The present model permits every single-qubit X, Y and Z coupling, so symmetry-protected results must be distinguished from this target.

The May construction’s proven version uses a randomized geometric embedding; its separate explicit variant lacks a complete lifetime proof. Efficient passive preparation and stability under arbitrary local Hamiltonian perturbations are also left for further work. These are additional requirements, beyond the fixed-Hamiltonian storage question formulated here.

The status distinction is useful for selecting research projects: the original existence target now requires assessment of the new theorem, while initialization, perturbation stability and alternative constructions remain separate directions. They should receive their own precise statements if added to the catalogue, rather than silently replacing the question under this identifier.

sentences: Passive quantum memory aims to preserve an encoded qubit through the natural dynamics of a material without repeated active correction.
The question here fixes a nonzero temperature and asks whether lifetime can grow without bound in a three-dimensional local stabilizer system.
Protecting a qubit requires retaining phase information as well as distinguishing its classical basis states.
The saved card records a May 2026 claimed affirmative construction, while distinguishing its proof claim from an independently verified conclusion.
This makes the record a useful guide to the precise thermal model and remaining verification questions rather than an unqualified assertion that the original existence problem is still open.
